```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(scales)
library(knitr)

# Read clean Florida demographic and boundary data created by download_data.R
fl_census   <- readRDS("data/fl_census.rds")
fl_tracts   <- readRDS("data/fl_tracts.rds")
us_counties <- readRDS("data/us_counties.rds")
```

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
### Milestone #5 Dataset Scale: Analyzing 5,100+ FL Tracts & 3,100+ US Counties
This study leverages massive demographic datasets from the U.S. Census Bureau's 2018–2022 American Community Survey (ACS) 5-Year Estimates across two geographic tiers:
- **Florida Census Tracts:** High-density neighborhood resolution across **`r comma(nrow(fl_tracts))`** tracts in all 67 Florida counties.
- **United States National Counties:** Nationwide comparative scale analyzing **`r comma(nrow(us_counties))`** counties across all 50 states, the District of Columbia, and Puerto Rico.
:::

## Florida Demographics: County & Neighborhood Patterns

### County-Level Distribution of Hispanic Population

The choropleth map below displays the geographic concentration of Hispanic and Latino residents across all 67 Florida counties.

```{r}
#| label: florida-choropleth
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-align: center

# Create choropleth map of Florida counties
ggplot(fl_census) +
  # Draw county polygons filled by Hispanic percentage with clean, crisp white borders
  geom_sf(aes(fill = hispanic_pct), color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  # Apply modern magma color palette with percentage labels
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    option = "magma",
    labels = label_percent(scale = 1, accuracy = 1),
    name = "Hispanic / Latino\nPopulation (%)"
  ) +
  # Clean map styling with no background clutter
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, hjust = 0),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey30", size = 11, hjust = 0, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    plot.caption = element_text(color = "grey40", size = 8.5, hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 12)),
    legend.position = "right",
    legend.title = element_text(size = 9.5, face = "bold"),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 8.5)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Hispanic Population Distribution in Florida",
    subtitle = "Percentage of county residents identifying as Hispanic or Latino (2018–2022 ACS)",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2018–2022 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates"
  )
```

### Florida Tract-Level Microdata (5,100+ Census Tracts)

Moving beyond county aggregates, the high-density scatter plot below plots over 5,000 individual Florida census tracts. Each point represents a neighborhood census tract, with point sizes scaled to total population, points colored by county, and a smoothed cyan trend line highlighting the non-linear relationship between median household income and Hispanic population share.

```{r}
#| label: florida-tract-scatter
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| fig-align: center

# Prepare Florida tract dataset joined with county names
fl_tracts_plot <- fl_tracts |>
  mutate(county_geoid = substr(GEOID, 1, 5)) |>
  left_join(
    fl_census |>
      st_drop_geometry() |>
      select(GEOID, county_name = NAME),
    by = c("county_geoid" = "GEOID")
  ) |>
  mutate(County = str_remove(county_name, " County, Florida")) |>
  filter(
    !is.na(hispanic_pct),
    !is.na(med_incomeE),
    !is.na(County),
    hispanic_pct >= 0,
    hispanic_pct <= 100,
    total_popE > 0,
    med_incomeE > 0
  )

# Plot income vs. Hispanic share for all 5,100+ Florida census tracts
ggplot(
  fl_tracts_plot,
  aes(x = med_incomeE, y = hispanic_pct)
) +
  # Draw tract points with alpha transparency to reveal dense neighborhood clustering
  geom_point(aes(size = total_popE, color = County), alpha = 0.35) +
  # Add cyan smoothed trend curve
  geom_smooth(color = "cyan", se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_color_viridis_d(option = "turbo", guide = "none") +
  scale_size_continuous(
    range = c(0.7, 4.5),
    trans = "sqrt",
    labels = label_comma(),
    name = "Tract Population"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Household Income vs. Hispanic Share across 5,100+ Florida Tracts",
    subtitle = paste0(
      comma(nrow(fl_tracts_plot)),
      " tracts | Size = population | Color = county | Cyan curve = smoothed loess trend"
    ),
    x = "Median Household Income",
    y = "Hispanic Population Share",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2018–2022 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey30", size = 10.5, margin = margin(b = 8)),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```

### Top 5 Florida Counties by Hispanic Share

The summary table below highlights the five Florida counties with the largest proportion of Hispanic residents:

```{r}
#| label: top-counties-table

# Prepare summary table of the top 5 Florida counties by Hispanic share
fl_census |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  mutate(County = str_remove(NAME, " County, Florida")) |>
  arrange(desc(hispanic_pct)) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  select(
    County,
    `Total Population` = total_popE,
    `Hispanic Population` = hispanicE,
    `Hispanic Share` = hispanic_pct
  ) |>
  mutate(
    `Total Population` = comma(`Total Population`),
    `Hispanic Population` = comma(`Hispanic Population`),
    `Hispanic Share` = percent(`Hispanic Share`, scale = 1, accuracy = 0.1)
  ) |>
  kable(
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"),
    caption = "Florida Counties with the Highest Hispanic Population Share"
  )
```

## National Demographics: 3,100+ U.S. Counties across Regions

### Nationwide Comparison: Income vs. Hispanic Share

To contextualize Florida's demographics within the broader American landscape, the high-density plot below analyzes over 3,100 U.S. counties. The data are faceted into the four official U.S. Census Regions—**Midwest**, **Northeast**, **South**, and **West**—revealing distinct regional economic and demographic alignments.

```{r}
#| label: us-counties-scatter
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 8.5
#| fig-align: center

# Filter national counties with valid economic and demographic observations
us_plot_data <- us_counties |>
  filter(
    !is.na(med_incomeE),
    !is.na(hispanic_pct),
    !is.na(region),
    region %in% c("Midwest", "Northeast", "South", "West")
  )

# High-density faceted regional comparison
ggplot(
  us_plot_data,
  aes(x = med_incomeE, y = hispanic_pct, color = region)
) +
  # Points sized by county population with alpha transparency for high density
  geom_point(aes(size = total_popE), alpha = 0.35) +
  # Smoothed regional loess trend curves
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, color = "grey25", linewidth = 0.9) +
  # Facet by U.S. Census Region
  facet_wrap(~region, ncol = 2) +
  scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2", guide = "none") +
  scale_size_continuous(
    range = c(0.8, 5.5),
    trans = "sqrt",
    labels = label_comma(),
    name = "County Population"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_dollar()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "National Income vs. Hispanic Population Distribution by Region",
    subtitle = paste0(
      "High-density analysis across ", comma(nrow(us_plot_data)),
      " U.S. counties | Faceted by U.S. Census Region with regional loess smooth curves"
    ),
    x = "Median Household Income",
    y = "Hispanic Population Share",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2018–2022 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    strip.background = element_rect(fill = "grey95", color = NA),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "grey30", size = 11, margin = margin(b = 10)),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )
```

### Regional Demographic Breakdown

The table below summarizes median household income, aggregate population, and average Hispanic population shares across the four U.S. regions:

```{r}
#| label: us-regional-summary-table

# Compute weighted economic and demographic indicators by region
us_plot_data |>
  group_by(`U.S. Region` = region) |>
  summarise(
    `Counties Analyzed` = n(),
    `Total Population` = sum(total_popE, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Weighted Median Income` = sum(med_incomeE * total_popE, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_popE, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Aggregate Hispanic Share` = (sum(hispanicE, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(total_popE, na.rm = TRUE)) * 100
  ) |>
  mutate(
    `Counties Analyzed` = comma(`Counties Analyzed`),
    `Total Population` = comma(`Total Population`),
    `Weighted Median Income` = dollar(`Weighted Median Income`),
    `Aggregate Hispanic Share` = percent(`Aggregate Hispanic Share`, scale = 1, accuracy = 0.1)
  ) |>
  kable(
    align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r"),
    caption = "Demographic Overview Across U.S. Census Regions (2018–2022 ACS)"
  )
```

## Comparative Demographic Insights

1. **State vs. National Dynamics:**
   Across the 3,144 U.S. counties, the West and South exhibit the highest concentrations of Hispanic residents, but their underlying relationships with income differ substantially. In the West, Hispanic populations are distributed broadly across both agricultural communities and affluent coastal counties. In the South, Florida functions as an exceptional demographic anchor where high Hispanic shares span the entire economic spectrum—from agricultural hubs in Hendry and Hardee counties to major metropolitan centers in Miami-Dade, Broward, and Orange counties.

2. **Neighborhood-Scale Nuance in Florida:**
   While county aggregates provide an essential high-level overview, analyzing 5,160 individual Florida tracts reveals tremendous internal heterogeneity. Many tracts in Miami-Dade and Osceola exceed 80% Hispanic concentration while spanning household incomes from under $25,000 to over $150,000. The non-linear cyan loess trend illustrates that Hispanic representation in Florida is not confined to low-income census tracts, reflecting the robust, multi-generational economic diversity of the state's Hispanic populace.

3. **Regional Continental Divergence:**
   In the Midwest and Northeast, the vast majority of counties report Hispanic shares below 10%, with elevated percentages tightly focused in specific urbanized manufacturing or transportation hubs. By contrast, Southern and Western counties exhibit substantial geographic clustering shaped by historic borders, migration channels, and expanding regional economic centers.
